marble.name: Chromosomes, Genes & DNA
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Describe the relationship between chromosomes, genes, and DNA in heredity, including the double helix structure of DNA and the historical roles of Watson, Crick, Franklin, and Wilkins
marble.prompt: If you was asked what DNA actually is and where it is in the body, could they explain the relationship between DNA, genes, and chromosomes — and say roughly how many chromosomes a human cell has?

cluster.summary: Your child is exploring how living things interact with their environment — learning about different habitats, simple food chains, and the difference between living, dead, and never-alive things.

misconceptions: Thinking a chromosome contains many separate pieces of DNA, rather than being ONE long coiled DNA molecule.
Treating genes, DNA and chromosomes as three separate kinds of thing rather than nested parts of one structure (gene = section of DNA; DNA coils into a chromosome).
Believing DNA/genes are only in special cells (e.g. sex cells or blood) rather than in the nucleus of nearly every body cell.
Confusing a gene (a section of DNA coding for a characteristic) with a whole chromosome, or with a single 'trait' with no physical basis.
Assuming Watson and Crick discovered DNA's structure alone, unaware that Franklin's and Wilkins's X-ray evidence was essential.
representations: A zoom/drill-down sequence: cell → nucleus → chromosome → unravelled DNA → highlighted gene, each level nested inside the last.
The double-helix 'twisted ladder' model with base pairs as rungs.
A coiled-rope analogy showing a chromosome as one long DNA molecule wound up tightly.
A karyotype image showing 23 pairs of human chromosomes.
Franklin's X-ray diffraction 'Photo 51' alongside the Watson–Crick model, illustrating evidence → model.
authoredAnswer: No. Nearly every body cell contains the SAME complete set of DNA — all 46 chromosomes (23 pairs), all the genes. Skin and muscle cells differ because they USE (express) different genes, not because they hold different ones. The hierarchy: DNA coils up into chromosomes inside the nucleus of the cell, and a gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein.

wrongAnswers.wrong: Yes — skin cells carry the skin genes and muscle cells carry the muscle genes, which is why they differ.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Agrees the cells differ because they hold different genes, rather than because they express different ones
wrongAnswers.fix: Establish genome constancy: every body cell came from the same fertilised egg by division and carries the same full DNA; differences come from which genes are switched on.

wrongAnswers.wrong: Genes are the biggest — chromosomes and DNA fit inside the genes.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Nests the levels the wrong way when asked to order them
wrongAnswers.fix: Rebuild the nesting concretely: a chromosome is one long coiled DNA molecule; a gene is a short section of that DNA; order from base to cell.

wrongAnswers.wrong: A gene is a tiny blueprint-picture of the feature it produces.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Describes a gene AS the trait or a miniature of the body part, not as coding for a protein
wrongAnswers.fix: Replace the picture with the code idea: a gene is an instruction that codes for a protein; proteins build and run the body, which is how genes affect features.
